newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German building jobs hit by long, hard winter.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German building jobs hit by long, hard winter.

text.p: German building unions and employers said on Thursday the huge January rise in joblessness in the industry was partly a consequence of the scrapping of "poor weather" payments to staff by the government last winter.
Germany's Federal Labour Office estimated earlier that winter unemployment in the country's construction-related industries accounted for nearly half of the 510,000 jump in January joblessness.
The increase means there are an estimated 400,000, or one in three, German builders unemployed.

The former poor weather payments, which the government cancelled from December 1995, were designed to compensate workers for lost income during hard weather, and were valued particularly highly in the building sector.
In their place, employer and union representatives were obliged to negotiate agreements under which firms pay their staff "bridging money" in times of poor weather.

"The bridging money agreements are too expensive for the firms and the vast majority do not pay them. It is cheaper for them to get rid of their staff during winter," a spokesman for IG Bau said by telephone.

The Zentralverband des deutschen Baugewerbes (ZDB), one of the main construction employer groups, also said the agreements were too high for firms already suffering what it called "an economic crisis", and said the issue would be high on the agenda of wage talks to start later this month.
Neither the ZDB nor IG Bau said any improvement in sector conditions was likely in the short-term, with the ZDB predicting a year-on-year rise of 60,000 unemployed in the sector during 1997.

Earlier it was announced that German unemployment surged to 4.66 million in January, the highest level since the Great Depression of the 1930s, with two-fifths of the increase coming from people in the construction industry.
Under the new bridging money agreements, employees should receive 75 percent of salary lost because of poor weather.

But despite the fact that part of that is paid for by the employee in reduced holiday pay, and the rest through funds set up for the purpose, it has been widely acknowledged that the burden on individual firms is too great.
Many firms simply reduce their core workforce during the winter months and use cheaper, foreign labourers instead.
IG Bau has already signalled that it sees poor weather compensation as one of the key issues in 1997 wage talks due to start on February 27 in Frankfurt.
It will also be seeking the reinstatement of the 13th-month end-of-year bonus and a reversal of a recent 20 percent cut in sick pay entitlements.
The union has also said it sees accords in the metal and engineering industry securing wage rises of 1.5 percent and 2.5 percent this year and next as "guiding indicators" in its negotiations.
